questions.q: List the six basic consumer rights as per the Consumer Protection Act.
questions.a: The six basic consumer rights are: (1) Right to Safety, (2) Right to be Informed, (3) Right to Choose, (4) Right to be Heard, (5) Right to Redressal, (6) Right to Consumer Education. A wrong answer (e.g., listing "Right to Refund" or "Right to Warranty" as a basic right) reveals that the student is confusing statutory rights with seller policies or specific remedies. The Act defines these six as fundamental; others like refund are modes of redressal, not independent rights.

questions.q: Explain in your own words what the "Right to be Informed" means and give one example where this right is violated.
questions.a: Right to be Informed means the consumer has the right to complete, accurate, and truthful information about the quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard, and price of goods or services, so they can make an informed decision. Example: A packaged food item does not declare the presence of allergens (e.g., peanuts) on its label. A wrong answer that says "Right to be Informed means the seller must tell me the price" is incomplete — it misses the broader scope (ingredients, expiry, warnings, terms of service) and confuses the right with a single piece of information.

questions.q: A consumer buys a "100% cotton" shirt that shrinks excessively after one wash. The label did not mention any pre-shrink treatment or care instructions. Which consumer right(s) are violated? Justify your answer.
questions.a: Two rights are violated: (1) Right to be Informed — the label failed to disclose material information (shrinkage tendency, care instructions) needed for proper use; (2) Right to Safety — if the garment becomes unwearable or causes skin irritation due to undisclosed chemical finishes, safety is compromised. A student who only picks "Right to be Informed" misses the safety dimension. A student who picks "Right to Redressal" confuses the violation with the remedy — redressal is the process to fix the violation, not the violation itself.

questions.q: Compare and contrast "Right to Choose" and "Right to be Heard". How do they operate at different stages of the consumer journey?
questions.a: Right to Choose operates at the pre-purchase stage: it ensures access to a variety of goods/services at competitive prices without coercion (e.g., no tie-in sales). Right to be Heard operates at the post-purchase stage: it guarantees that consumer complaints and interests are considered in appropriate forums (e.g., consumer courts, company grievance cells). A wrong answer that says both are about "having options" conflates choice (market variety) with voice (participation in policy/grievance). The distinction is critical for board questions asking "At which stage does this right apply?"

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The Right to Consumer Education is the most important right because it enables the exercise of all other rights." Support your evaluation with two arguments.
questions.a: The statement is largely valid. Argument 1: Without awareness of their rights (e.g., knowing that "no refund" boards are illegal), consumers cannot invoke Right to Redressal or Right to be Heard. Argument 2: Education helps consumers interpret information (Right to be Informed), recognize unsafe products (Right to Safety), and demand variety (Right to Choose). A weak answer that says "Yes, because education is important" lacks specific linkage to the other five rights. The evaluation must show the enabling relationship.

questions.q: Design a poster for a school campaign that illustrates any three consumer rights using only symbols/icons (no text). Provide a legend explaining each symbol and the right it represents.
questions.a: A good answer includes: (1) A shield with a checkmark → Right to Safety (protection from hazardous goods). (2) A magnifying glass over a label → Right to be Informed (access to complete information). (3) A gavel or balance scale → Right to Redressal (access to justice). A poor answer uses generic icons (e.g., a shopping bag for "Right to Choose" without showing variety) or fails to distinguish between rights visually. This tests whether the student can distill each right to its core essence — a skill needed for board project work and CUET visual literacy questions.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Consumer rights are the fundamental ______ guaranteed to every consumer under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (and previously the 1986 Act) to ensure fair trade practices, protect against exploitation, and empower consumers in the marketplace.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you buy a new smartphone online, but when it arrives, the screen is ______ and the charger is missing.
What is Consumer rights? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Consumer rights are the fundamental entitlements guaranteed to every consumer under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (and previously the 1986 Act) to ensure fair trade practices, protect against exploitation, and empower consumers in the marketplace.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Consumer rights?
questions.a: Students often think "Right to Redressal" means an automatic right to a full refund or replacement in every complaint.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can accurately list all six consumer rights, explain each right with a distinct real-life example, and identify which right is violated in a given consumer complaint scenario.
